comparison: Both evaluate V4 recording data showing differential L1 effects across branches (C43-C51). OpenEval finds this strongly supports refutation of flat models with global inhibition (P < 10^-4). Peer reviewers acknowledge the finding but note interpretational disagreement in Round 2, with H&M arguing the data is 'most compatible with the flat model' while authors argue it refutes flat models. Reviewers request clarification on 'localized activations' vs 'selection signals.'

Both address V1 recording data showing temporal precedence of L1 over L2 selection signals (C52-C54, C77-C79). OpenEval finds this strongly supports serial processing and refutes flat models. Peer reviewers question the relevance and interpretation, asking for clarification on 'how the gradual spread of object-based attention in mental curve tracing tasks relate to hierarchical decision-making' and why this 'cannot be explained by flat models.'

Both evaluate human L3 addition experiment showing increased seriality (C84, C93-C94). OpenEval finds this supports the existence of independent decision machinery. Peer reviewers question whether this necessarily implies the two-branch task requires hierarchical processing, suggesting 'subjects' strategy shifts from a flat process to a hierarchical process as the number of branching points increases.'

Both address L1-L2 interactions and mechanism claims (C55-C62). OpenEval finds the reasoning sound and appropriately caveated, noting interactions don't distinguish between model types. Peer reviewers accept the finding of interactions but request more direct treatment of H&M's claim about 'extra modulatory signal' that 'must be carefully tuned,' suggesting acceptance but wanting more careful interpretation.

Both evaluate simulation results and RT analysis comparing H&M model to monkey data (C34-C42 overlap, with R1 also including C69-C71). OpenEval finds clear discrepancies supporting refutation of flat models. Peer reviewers raise concerns about RT analysis, noting 'the task did not have a reaction time design' and that 'additional mechanisms, such as a collapsing decision bound might make a flat model compatible with the RT data.' In Round 2, they note H&M produced a compatible version.

Both address critical model dependencies lacking neurophysiological support (C63-C68 overlap). OpenEval finds the evaluation comprehensive and conclusion well-justified. Peer reviewers question whether these features are truly incompatible, noting in Round 2 that H&M 'produce a version of the model that reproduces the L1 dependence and realistic mean RTs, using a kind of collapsing bound' that addresses some concerns.

Both address neurophysiological compatibility of H&M model's exponential activity and self-excitation (C28-C33). OpenEval finds the logical chain from model features to neurophysiological incompatibility well-supported. Peer reviewers did not explicitly challenge these arguments but requested authors make more explicit that 'sensory neural responses provide only indirect evidence' and to 'interpret the neural responses with caution.'

Both address model fitting and behavioral analysis showing flat model predictions vs monkey data (C4, C10-C12, C19 overlap). OpenEval finds the logic sound and comparison clear. Peer reviewers acknowledge these as basis for discussion, accepting the basic findings but requesting the paper 'more directly address whether the data in the original submission by Lorteije et al. exclude a flat model with inhibition,' indicating uncertainty about interpretation.

Both address flexibility in parallel vs serial processing and flat model limitations (C87-C90 overlap). OpenEval finds the argument well-constructed across multiple experimental conditions. Peer reviewers question whether flexibility data necessarily supports hierarchical over flat models, noting 'subjects' strategy shifts from a flat process to a hierarchical process as the number of branching points increases,' suggesting the conclusion may be premature.

Both reference prior study methods and findings (C2-C3 overlap). OpenEval finds these appropriately cited factual descriptions. Peer reviewers acknowledge these findings as basis for discussion, accepting the primary conclusion about hierarchical processing but requesting more direct address of whether data exclude flat models.

OpenEval evaluated claims C73, C75-C76 summarizing prior published work (Pooresmaeili and Roelfsema 2014; Houtkamp et al. 2003) as appropriately cited factual descriptions. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific contextual claims.

OpenEval evaluated claims C85-C86 about training effects and persistence of serial processing as supported by straightforward empirical observation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims about practice effects.

OpenEval evaluated methodological details (C95-C104) including ethical compliance, sample sizes, recording sites, and stimulus parameters as appropriate factual statements for reproducibility. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these methodological claims.

OpenEval evaluated general statement about decision-making (C1) and main conclusion (C6) as supported by accumulated evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these framing claims.

OpenEval evaluated claim C72 about fundamental property of flat models as valid inference about model structure. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing this architectural claim.
